article_title: Empowering ChatGPT with guidance mechanism in blended learning: effect of self-regulated learning, higher-order thinking skills, and knowledge construction
citation: Lee, H.-Y., Chen, P.-H., Wang, W.-S., Huang, Y.-M., & Wu, T.-T. (2024). Empowering ChatGPT with guidance mechanism in blended learning: effect of self-regulated learning, higher-order thinking skills, and knowledge construction. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 21, 16. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-024-00447-4
title: Guidance-based ChatGPT-assisted Learning Aid (GCLA)
description: The GCLA is an educational tool for blended learning that fuses ChatGPT (the gpt-3.5-turbo-16 k model, max_tokens 4000, temperature 0.6, presence_penalty 0.2) with Apple's Shortcuts on iOS 12+ devices. Its defining behavior is that "Rather than giving direct answers, GCLA prompts students to formulate their own, offering insightful hints to aid problem-solving." Learners must submit a question together with their own proposed answer before receiving guidance, and a learning log file records all questions and answers to support reflection and retention.
requirements: Learners must obtain an OpenAI authentication key and submit their own proposed answer before receiving ChatGPT guidance
Runs on Apple devices with iOS 12 or above via Apple's Shortcuts
constraints: The study's comparison used the GPT-3.5 iteration of ChatGPT on iOS due to its predominant use and use in GCLA's development
examples: In the article's worked example, a student entered a propane combustion problem with an unbalanced initial equation, received a hint that the answer was incorrect, counted atoms, revised to C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O, and had the corrected answer corroborated by the app
key_sources: Lee, H.-Y., Chen, P.-H., Wang, W.-S., Huang, Y.-M., & Wu, T.-T. (2024). Empowering ChatGPT with guidance mechanism in blended learning: effect of self-regulated learning, higher-order thinking skills, and knowledge construction. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 21, 16. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-024-00447-4

article_title: Inclusive and effective teaching of Nature-Based Social Prescribing for allied health professional students within digital environments.
citation: Pywell S., Wallace C., Wallace S., Davies M. (2025). Inclusive and effective teaching of Nature-Based Social Prescribing for allied health professional students within digital environments. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1694834
title: Group Concept Mapping as a coproduction framework for inclusive pedagogy exploration
description: Group Concept Mapping (GCM) is defined in the article as a "structured methodology for organizing the ideas of a group on any topic of interest and presenting those visually through a series of interrelated maps". It integrates participatory, quantitative and qualitative methods: brainstorming generates statements, participants sort and rate them, and multidimensional scaling with Ward's-method hierarchical cluster analysis yields visual theme maps and Go Zone quadrants. The article uses GCM via the groupwisdom tool to coproduce priorities for inclusive NbSP teaching with 38 stakeholders, arguing it frees participants from groupthink constraints of Delphi approaches.
requirements: Anonymous participation and independent stage completion
Sequential mixed methods: sorting before rating
Consolidation of brainstormed statements following published GCM guidance (100-statement maximum)
constraints: Attrition threatens internal validity and must be transparently reported
Results are representative of participants who took part, not generalizable to the wider stakeholder population
Cognitive loading of participants due to task complexity is a known limitation
target_learning_goals: Stakeholder-generated curriculum content priorities for nature-based social prescribing
examples: The study brainstormed 158 statements consolidated to 100, sorted by 10 participants above the 75% threshold, rated by 9, with a stress value of 0.3332 within the reliable 0.21–0.37 range
key_sources: Pywell S., Wallace C., Wallace S., Davies M. (2025). Inclusive and effective teaching of Nature-Based Social Prescribing for allied health professional students within digital environments. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1694834

article_title: Embedding simulation in genetic counselor education from the first week of training: Learning outcomes, standardized clients, and students' satisfaction.
citation: Jacobs, C., & McEwen, A. (2025). Embedding simulation in genetic counselor education from the first week of training: Learning outcomes, standardized clients, and students' satisfaction. Journal of Genetic Counseling, 34, e1857. https://doi.org/10.1002/jgc4.1857
title: Co-designed simulation learning outcomes and standardized clients for genetic counselor education
description: A set of six simulation learning outcomes and eight standardized clients built with experienced genetic counselors using co-design principles for a master of genetic counseling program. The outcomes cover "establishing an effective counseling relationship, eliciting information, assessing need, delivering difficult news and helping clients cope with complex emotions, effective communication and facilitating adaptation". Real cases were de-identified into detailed case studies, mapped to learning outcomes and program stages, and sequenced from straightforward to complex across the two-year program.
requirements: Standardized clients must be reviewed for accuracy, authenticity, and privacy by the genetic counselors involved in the real cases
The authors state regular review and update of the standardized clients is vitally important to optimize learning
constraints: The authors question the extent to which outcomes around communicating effectively and facilitating adaptation can be achieved in a brief simulated interaction
Further work may be needed to validate each standardized client for each learning outcome
target_learners: first-year master of genetic counseling students (novice student genetic counselors)
target_learning_goals: delivering difficult news and helping clients cope with complex emotions
examples: Eight real cases addressing direct-to-consumer testing, variants of uncertain significance, unexpected results, prenatal diagnosis and complex family dynamics were developed into eight standardized clients
The two most straightforward scenarios were selected for the first teaching block
key_sources: Jacobs, C., & McEwen, A. (2025). Embedding simulation in genetic counselor education from the first week of training: Learning outcomes, standardized clients, and students' satisfaction. Journal of Genetic Counseling, 34, e1857. https://doi.org/10.1002/jgc4.1857

article_title: The acceptance and impact of Google Classroom integrating into a clinical pathology course for nursing students: A technology acceptance model approach.
citation: Huang Tzu-Hao, Liu Fen, Chen Li-Chen, Tsai Ching-Ching. (2021). The acceptance and impact of Google Classroom integrating into a clinical pathology course for nursing students: A technology acceptance model approach. PLoS ONE 16(3): e0247819. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0247819
title: Google Classroom clinical pathology course platform with five themed activity zones
description: The article describes a Google Classroom platform built for 12 units of a clinical pathology course, where "Each unit included separate 'zones' for Videos, News, Games, Quizzes, and Arena." The Video zone linked to teacher-made or YouTube videos; the News zone linked pathology knowledge to everyday life; the Games zone used Quizlet, Quizizz, and Quizalize with time-based leader boards; the Quizzes zone provided past national exam papers via Google Drive and Google Forms with instant feedback; and the Arena zone supported competition, discussion, and teacher commentary. Students used their own internet-enabled mobile devices to access it anytime.
requirements: Students need internet-enabled devices and access (free campus/dorm wireless was provided for those without unlimited internet), and time to learn to operate the platform
constraints: Students faced problems similar to other learning management systems, such as internet speed and coverage, difficulty understanding platform operation, and needing time to practice
target_learners: fourth-grade five-year junior college nursing students in Taiwan
target_learning_goals: clinical pathology knowledge (microbiology, immunology, bloodwork, system diseases, function tests, tumor markers)
examples: During Weeks 3–18 the experimental group received one hour/week of GC-integrated activities, including 10- to 15-minute activities in each of the five themed zones
key_sources: Huang Tzu-Hao, Liu Fen, Chen Li-Chen, Tsai Ching-Ching. (2021). The acceptance and impact of Google Classroom integrating into a clinical pathology course for nursing students: A technology acceptance model approach. PLoS ONE 16(3): e0247819. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0247819

article_title: The perceived effects of faculty presence vs. absence on small-group learning and group dynamics: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Hoffman M, Wilkinson JE, Xu J, Wiecha J. (2014). The perceived effects of faculty presence vs. absence on small-group learning and group dynamics: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-014-0258-1
title: 16-item self-rating survey derived from the Group Climate Questionnaire-Short version for small-group process
description: A survey instrument used to have students self-score and self-rate learning, group participation and dynamics. It was 'derived from the Group Climate Questionnaire – Short version (GCQ-S)' using three GCQ-S items plus eight items from Steele et al, yielding '16 Likert scaled questions', plus questions about group size and perceived full participation. Students completed one survey after a faculty-present ('in') case and one after a faculty-absent ('out') case for paired comparison.
requirements: Requires paired completion with a matching identifier so 'in' and 'out' surveys can be linked for paired analysis
constraints: Items are self-reported perceptions, not observed behavior; the authors note some absolute differences in scores were small
target_learners: Medical students in small-group clerkship sessions
target_learning_goals: Assessment of group dynamics, group learning process, participation, and perceived case-discussion outcomes
examples: Students rated items such as 'Utilized the knowledge of students in the group' and 'The members depended upon the faculty leader for direction' on 5-point Likert scales after each studied case.
key_sources: Hoffman M, Wilkinson JE, Xu J, Wiecha J. (2014). The perceived effects of faculty presence vs. absence on small-group learning and group dynamics: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-014-0258-1

article_title: From Individual Prompts to Collective Intelligence: Mainstreaming Generative AI in the Classroom
citation: Junaid Qadir and Muhammad Salman Khan. (2026). From Individual Prompts to Collective Intelligence: Mainstreaming Generative AI in the Classroom. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06171
title: Generative Collective Intelligence (GCI) framework: AI as a cognitive bridge within collective human reasoning
description: The paper's central theoretical proposal adapts Kehler, Page, Pentland, Reeves, and Brown's Generative Collective Intelligence framework for engineering classrooms. The framework "rejects the view of intelligence as an isolated, algorithmic property and instead understands it as fundamentally social, relational, and collectively constructed", positioning AI in dual roles as an interactive computational agent and as a technology that organizes collective knowledge. In the authors' implementation, AI is consulted only after human reasoning establishes a foundation, serving as "a cognitive bridge rather than a replacement tutor". Students experience AI as one voice among many, interrogated through collective judgment.
requirements: Human reasoning must establish the collective foundation before AI is consulted; AI consultation is tied to specific purposes such as surfacing perspectives or critiquing preliminary analyses.
constraints: The authors state this represents "one possible implementation among many, designed specifically for our context and constraints".
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness of when AI adds value
examples: Two 50-minute sessions in DCCN-I and S&S at Qatar University where Question Sorts and Peel the Fruit preceded two strategically timed AI consultations, and exit tickets asked how the group's collective intelligence changed after consulting GenAI.
key_sources: Junaid Qadir and Muhammad Salman Khan. (2026). From Individual Prompts to Collective Intelligence: Mainstreaming Generative AI in the Classroom. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06171

article_title: From Individual Prompts to Collective Intelligence: Mainstreaming Generative AI in the Classroom
citation: Junaid Qadir and Muhammad Salman Khan. (2026). From Individual Prompts to Collective Intelligence: Mainstreaming Generative AI in the Classroom. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06171
title: Five-element GCI activity pattern: human reasoning first, strategic AI consultation, critical evaluation, artifact creation, metacognitive reflection
description: A repeatable lesson-level sequence the authors operationalize across two 50-minute class sessions. Activities begin with individual thinking and pair/group collaboration using thinking routines, after which "only after human reasoning establishes foundation do groups consult AI for specific purposes (surfacing additional perspectives, critiquing preliminary analyses, generating alternative approaches)". Groups then interrogate AI outputs against their collective reasoning, produce tangible artifacts such as concept maps and layered diagrams, and close with explicit reflection on what humans contribute that AI cannot. The pattern holds AI as an enhancer rather than a replacement of collective human intelligence.
requirements: AI consultation must occur after human question generation and initial analysis, and explicit metacognitive framing must be provided throughout.
constraints: The authors describe it as one possible implementation designed for their context and constraints; the reported evidence is two sessions without control groups.
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students in group work
examples: Groups generated and sorted questions (clarifying versus generative), consulted a CustomGPT or ChatGPT with the prompt structure "Summarize multiple perspectives on...", built three-layer Peel the Fruit diagrams, then asked AI what ethical issues were missing.
key_sources: Junaid Qadir and Muhammad Salman Khan. (2026). From Individual Prompts to Collective Intelligence: Mainstreaming Generative AI in the Classroom. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06171

article_title: Enhancing Agent Communication and Learning through Action and Language
citation: Hugo Caselles-Dupré, Olivier Sigaud, Mohamed Chetouani. (2023). Show and Tell: Enhancing Agent Communication and Learning through Action and Language. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10842
title: Goal-conditioned teacher-learner agents with Bayesian Goal Inference for pedagogy and pragmatism
description: The article introduces a novel family of goal-conditioned agents (GC-agents) that can act both as teachers and learners, leveraging action with demonstrations and language with instructions as two communication modalities. The communication process works as follows: the teacher delivers a teaching signal (demonstration or instruction), and the learner, "employing Bayesian Goal Inference, attempts to predict the underlying goal associated with the teaching signal", retrying until it infers the goal. Demonstrations are added to the learner's replay buffer; instructions provide a curriculum of subgoals; the learner then pursues the predicted goal and updates its policy with reinforcement learning. Introducing goals is what enables pedagogy from the teacher side and pragmatism from the learner side.
requirements: Agents must be goal-conditioned, able to address a variety of goals
The learner must be able to infer goals from teaching signals via Bayesian Goal Inference
Policy updates via reinforcement learning techniques
constraints: Evaluated in the Fetch Block Stacking environment (stacking three cubes in configurations including pyramids and stacks)
target_learning_goals: learning to stack cubes in goal configurations; effective communication and teaching between agents
examples: The pedagogical teacher learns to predict the goals of its demonstrations, enabling more targeted instruction; the pragmatic learner learns to predict the goals of its own behavior, enhancing its preparation for communication.
key_sources: Hugo Caselles-Dupré, Olivier Sigaud, Mohamed Chetouani. (2023). Show and Tell: Enhancing Agent Communication and Learning through Action and Language. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10842
